cards.explanation: The answer is that he lays siege to it. Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon brings his entire army and lays siege to Jerusalem (Jeremiah 39:1). A siege means he parks the army at the city and settles in. Nobody brings an entire army just to say hello.

The answer is breached. On the ninth day of the fourth month of Zedekiah's eleventh year, the city was breached (Jeremiah 39:2). Zedekiah is the king of Judah, and the verse doesn't say how it happened. It just says the city was breached.

The answer is the Middle Gate. The king of Babylon's officials came in and sat there (Jeremiah 39:3). Nergal-sharezer, Nebo-sarsekim and the rest of the officials took their seats in that gate. The verse names several of them.

The answer is False. The text says that when Zedekiah and all the soldiers saw the officials, they fled (Jeremiah 39:4). They didn't walk up and surrender. They left the city, and they didn't wait around to talk about it.

The answer is True. Verse 4 says Zedekiah and his soldiers left the city at night. They went out by way of the king's garden, through the gate between the two walls. They also took the route to the Arabah.

The answer is Jericho. The army of the Chaldeans, which is Babylon's army, caught up with Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho (Jeremiah 39:5). They overtook him and seized him. Running at night through the dark did not get him away.

The answer is Riblah in the land of Hamath. The Chaldeans seized Zedekiah and brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar there (Jeremiah 39:5). That's where the king of Babylon was, and that's where he pronounced judgment. This is where the story gets heavy.

The answer is Babylon. Zedekiah was bound with bronze chains to be taken there (Jeremiah 39:7). It's the city of the king who defeated him. I think this is a hard place to stop and sit with for a second.

The answer is the king's palace and the people's houses. The Chaldeans set fire to the palace of the king and to the houses of the people (Jeremiah 39:8). Two kinds of buildings are named there. Those are the ones the verse says burned.
The answer is walls. The Chaldeans broke down the walls of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 39:8). The walls had kept Babylon outside for a long time, and now they were down. The siege had come to its end.

The answer is poor. Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, left behind in the land of Judah some of the poor people who had no property (Jeremiah 39:10). Then he gave them vineyards and fields. People with no property were given land.

The answer is True. At that time Nebuzaradan gave the poor people he left behind vineyards and fields (Jeremiah 39:10). People with no property were handed land to work. I bet that was quite a day for them.

The answer is to look after him and let no harm come to him. Nebuchadnezzar's orders were, "Take him, look after him, and do not let any harm come to him…" (Jeremiah 39:12). Jeremiah is the LORD's prophet, and he had been confined in the courtyard of the guard. The king of Babylon gave an order to protect him.
The answer is True. The orders end with, "do for him whatever he says." (Jeremiah 39:12). Nebuchadnezzar told Nebuzaradan to follow Jeremiah's lead. A king gave a prophet that kind of say.

The answer is to take him home. The officials turned Jeremiah over to Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, to take him home (Jeremiah 39:14). So Jeremiah remained among his own people. That's the simple, good ending to his time in the courtyard.

The answer is that His words against the city will be fulfilled. The LORD said, "I am about to fulfill My words against this city for harm and not for good…" (Jeremiah 39:16). The message was for Ebed-melech the Cushite. The LORD said He would do what He had said.

The answer is False. The LORD told Ebed-melech the Cushite, "But I will deliver you on that day, declares the LORD, and you will not be delivered into the hands of the men whom you fear." (Jeremiah 39:17). The men he feared would not get him. The LORD was the one doing the delivering.

The answer is because he trusted in the LORD. The LORD said, "Because you have trusted in Me, you will escape with your life like a spoil of war, declares the LORD." (Jeremiah 39:18). Ebed-melech the Cushite trusted Him, and the LORD gave him a promise. Trust is the reason the text gives.
